name: Hudson Valley Dutch

revival_periods.note: The revival largely bypassed the steep-gabled stone house in favour of the New Jersey gambrel; the Hudson type survives more in preservation than in imitation.

regions: Albany and Rensselaer counties, New York
Greene and Columbia counties, New York
Dutchess and Orange counties, New York
geography.hearth: the limestone belt of Ulster County — Kingston, Hurley, New Paltz — and the Beverwijck (Albany) region upriver

lineage.note: The town houses of Kingston and Albany reproduce the Netherlandish parapeted street gable with vlechtingen brick tumbling and iron beam anchors almost without modification.

description.short: The one-and-a-half-storey stone house of the mid and upper Hudson: two to two-and-a-half feet of coursed limestone, a steep unbroken gable, gable-end hearths, and a plate you can touch.
description.long:
The Hudson Valley Dutch house is what happens when a timber-framing culture meets a valley full of workable stone. In Holland the H-bent frame with its wedged anchor beams was the whole structure and brick or plank merely infilled it; in Ulster County the settlers found bedded limestone that split into courses with almost no dressing, and within a generation the frame retreated indoors while the wall became the structure. What survives from the frame is the room — a bent-spacing rhythm of eighteen to twenty-two feet — and the anchor beams themselves, which continue to be built into stone houses purely as floor framing, their through-tenons still projecting past the posts because that is how a Dutch carpenter made a beam land.

The hearth is the other survival, and it is the one that surprises people. The jambless fireplace has no cheeks: the fire burns on a raised hearth against a flat plastered wall, and a hood of plaster on lath or of timber, sometimes trimmed with a valance of chintz or leather, hangs above it on iron rods. There is no chimney breast projecting into the room. It draws badly by English standards and radiates superbly, and it makes the fire an object in the room rather than a recess in it. Jean Hasbrouck's house at New Paltz retains the only original eighteenth-century example on Huguenot Street, and standing before it explains more about Dutch domestic life than any inventory.

The exterior logic is austere and rational. The wall is twenty to thirty inches thick, laid in wide beds of shell-lime mortar, dressed and coursed on the entrance elevation and left as rubble on the other three — a house with one good face, which tells you exactly how much of the building was for looking at. The plate sits seven to nine feet above the floor, so the roof, forty-five to fifty-five degrees and unbroken, is most of the elevation. Chimneys are at or inside the gable ends. Windows are small, casement and leaded in the seventeenth century, replaced by nine-over-nine sash in the eighteenth, and set with iron shutter pintles still visible in the stone. After about 1700 the eave begins to spring: the lower rafters run past the wall face on a shallow concave curve, throwing water eighteen to twenty-four inches clear of the masonry.

In the towns the same culture builds in brick with the gable to the street, stepped or spouted, its raking edge finished with mouse-tooth tumbling, and studded with wrought-iron beam anchors that sometimes spell out a date. Nothing about that elevation is American; it is Amsterdam, moved. To stand inside one of the rural houses is to be in a single low room lit from two sides, with the anchor beams overhead at seven and a half feet, a flat wall at one end where the fire is, and two feet of stone between you and a Hudson Valley January.

defining_characteristics: Load-bearing coursed limestone or sandstone walls 20–30 in thick, dressed on the entrance elevation and rubble elsewhere
Steep unbroken side-gable roof at 45–55 degrees, springing from a plate 7–9 ft above the floor
Chimneys at or within the gable end walls, serving jambless fireplaces with suspended hoods
Exposed transverse anchor beams with projecting wedged through-tenons carrying the upper floor
Dutch doors divided horizontally, with the upper leaf glazed on later work
Wrought-iron beam anchors visible on the masonry gable, sometimes forming a date
A flared or 'spring' eave projecting 18–24 in on a concave sweep, on work after c. 1700
diagnostic_tells: A flat, unbroken chimney wall in the principal room with no projecting breast — the jambless fireplace, or its ghost
Coursed ashlar on one elevation, rubble on the other three
Anchor-beam tenons projecting through the posts, visible from below
Iron anchors and date irons on the gable masonry
Roof volume exceeding wall volume in the elevation, with second-floor windows either absent or set in the gable only

distinguished_from.difference: The Jersey branch uses a gambrel roof, red-brown Newark sandstone, and a pronounced concave spring eave that becomes a porch. The Hudson branch uses a steep straight gable, grey limestone, and a spring eave that is a water-shedding device rather than a shelter.

The revival is a gambrel house with a full-width shed dormer, a wood frame, symmetrical fenestration and a straight overhanging eave. The Hudson Dutch house has none of those things — no gambrel in its earliest and best work, no dormers, no symmetry obligation, and a stone wall thick enough to sit in the window reveal.

Both are thick-walled steep-roofed stone traditions. The German house has a central chimney serving a closed jamb stove and an asymmetric three-room plan; the Dutch house has gable-end hearths, open jambless fires and a one- or two-room plan.

proportional_system.governing_logic: The H-bent span carried over into masonry: rooms one bent deep, the house lengthened by adding bents along the ridge.
typical_ratios: Room depth 18–22 ft; overall 30–46 ft long × 20–24 ft deep
Wall thickness 20–30 in; wall height to plate 7–9 ft, giving 1:4 to 1:5 thickness to height
Spring eave projection 18–24 in with a sweep radius of 5–9 ft
Window opening 2 ft 6 in – 3 ft 2 in × 4 ft 0 in – 5 ft 0 in, glazed area under 10% of wall area
proportional_system.bay_rhythm: Additive and unequal — two, three or five openings across the eave front, with the door placed by the plan rather than by the composition until Georgian symmetry arrives after 1750.

massing_affinities.note: Two rooms with gable hearths, no passage.
The one-bent house, expanded by adding bents.
Late eighteenth-century Hudson work adopts the gambrel from the south.
Post-1750 Anglicization behind an unchanged section.
The Kingston and Albany urban gable-to-street house.

constraints.statement: Wall not less than 20 in of coursed load-bearing stone; window and door reveals must express the full wall depth. Stone veneer over frame produces a different building and reads as such at every opening.
Wall plate 7 ft 0 in to 9 ft 0 in above the finished floor, and roof pitch 12:12 to 17:12. If the plate rises or the pitch drops, the roof stops dominating and the type dissolves.

test.note: Tests the roof pitch clause. Wall plate height (7-9ft) is the same statement's other numeric claim, already tested on the parent dutch-colonial-american node, and stays prose here.

constraints.statement: Chimneys at or within the gable end walls. A central stack is a New England device and is incompatible with the open one- or two-room Dutch plan.
Spring eave, where used, projects 18–24 in on a concave sweep, not as a straight overhang, and only on work of c. 1700 or later. Below 12 in it does no work; a straight soffit is not a spring eave.

Openings: leaded casement with iron pintles to c. 1720; nine-over-nine or nine-over-six sash thereafter. Total glazed area under 10% of wall area. Dormers, where present at all, are small individual gabled ones, never continuous.

test.note: Tests the glazed-area clause. The sash/casement-by-date clause is date-conditional (OQ 22, no date-conditional resolution exists yet) and stays prose.

exemplars.name: Pieter Bronck House
exemplars.note: Thick stone walls, steep straight gable, single open chambers on two floors — the type before the gambrel and before Anglicization.

exemplars.name: Jean Hasbrouck House
exemplars.location: Historic Huguenot Street, New Paltz, New York
exemplars.note: National Historic Landmark. Retains the only original 18th-century jambless fireplace on Huguenot Street; built by Huguenots in wholly Dutch technique.

exemplars.name: Abraham Hasbrouck House
exemplars.location: Historic Huguenot Street, New Paltz, New York
exemplars.note: Multi-phase stone house whose successive campaigns are legible in the masonry — a good demonstration of additive bent-by-bent growth.

exemplars.name: Dyckman Farmhouse
exemplars.note: Late example: fieldstone lower storey, frame above, gambrel roof with a sprung eave carried on posts as a porch — the moment the eave becomes a porch.

sources: Helen Wilkinson Reynolds, Dutch Houses in the Hudson Valley before 1776 (1929)
Roderic H. Blackburn and Ruth Piwonka, Remembrance of Patria: Dutch Arts and Culture in Colonial America (1988)
Rosalie Fellows Bailey, Pre-Revolutionary Dutch Houses and Families in Northern New Jersey and Southern New York (1936)
Virginia Savage McAlester, A Field Guide to American Houses (2nd ed., 2013)

proportion_packs.note: BOUND FOR THE EAVE AND NOT FOR THE GAMBREL, and the distinction is this pack's opening finding. This node has a sprung eave -- 18-24 in projection on a 5-9 ft sweep radius -- over a STRAIGHT gable at 12:12 to 17:12, and its own distinguished_from entry says it outright: 'the Jersey branch uses a gambrel roof... a pronounced concave spring eave... the Hudson branch uses a steep straight gable.' So the two devices the pack carries are independent, which is why it names both in its title rather than calling itself 'the Dutch roof'. Read the eave rules here -- projection, flare start, sweep radius -- and leave the gambrel_section assembly, the break point and the two slope ratios alone; the straight-gable pitch this node gives is its own and is not in this pack.

The bent-spacing rhythm is explicitly what survives the shift from frame to masonry, per the style's own long description: 'What survives from the frame is the room — a bent-spacing rhythm of eighteen to twenty-two feet — and the anchor beams themselves, which continue to be built into stone houses purely as floor framing.' hudson-valley-dutch is named directly in timber-bay's own applies_to. The historic 18-22 ft room sits close enough to the pack's documented 16-20 ft English depth_and_pile band to use its rule directly, even though the framing culture it derives from (English box framing) is not the one that produced this variant's anchor-beam bents.

This is the stone-house variant proper — 20-30 in coursed limestone or sandstone, dressed and coursed on the entrance elevation, rubble on the other three — exactly the front/flank grading brick-course's own conflicts section describes for Westover and Carter's Grove. Bound at higher weight than the parent style's own binding because masonry is this variant's near-universal walling, not merely common. Where the openings are not dressed, read the pack's window_head_masonry rules as an upper bound on regularity rather than a description of what was built. hudson-valley-dutch is named directly in the pack's own applies_to.

hudson-valley-dutch is named directly in the pack's own applies_to. The hall-and-parlor plan with gable hearths and no passage is the pack's own paradigm case of a room sized by span, hearth reach and daylight rather than by ratio.

The style's own text gives the dated sequence directly — leaded casement to c. 1720, nine-over-nine or nine-over-six thereafter — which is exactly sash-light's light-count-from-glass-supply logic, and dates the surviving sash independently of the house. Bound for the light-count and muntin arithmetic only: this variant's own typical_ratios give window openings of roughly 1.4-1.7:1, well under sash-light's 1.85-2.6 measured Anglo-American band, and that divergence should be read as a real difference in vernacular Hudson Valley window shape rather than corrected toward the pack's figure.

This variant's own text places Georgian symmetry later and more reluctantly than its Jersey sibling: post-1750 Anglicization is listed only as 'possible' in the massing affinities, and the variant's own proportional_system still calls its bay rhythm 'additive and unequal... until Georgian symmetry arrives after 1750.' Bound optional and at low precedence for that late minority of Anglicized Hudson Valley houses only.
